digest.definition: A broad subject of many disciplines, practice-based and student-centred, in which making and creative inquiry are both how students learn and how they show their learning
distinctiveFeatures: A broad subject of many disciplines, practice-based and student-centred, in which making and creative inquiry are both how students learn and how they show their learning
Its practices conceive, test, make and share work that shapes visual and material culture, drawing on visual, spatial and sensory languages
Studios and workshops shape learning; flexible and online modes now sit beside them
It is increasingly interdisciplinary, crossing into the humanities, business, engineering, computing, health and the built environment
Contextual and critical study (history, theory, discourse) runs through practice rather than beside it
Assessment looks at process as well as product, often holistically, with feedback through reviews or crits
Live briefs, exhibitions, placements and partnerships tie learning to creative careers

themesInSubject.inThisSubject: headed equity, diversity and inclusion: diverse practices and student voices as a driver of creativity, decolonial attention to the subject's knowledge traditions, studio culture as an inclusive community, inclusive assessment; at the rungs, ethics and unequal representation; at master's, equity-centred creative strategy (D1, 1.10 to 1.16; 3.17 to 3.19; 4.4; 4.7)

the Equality Act duty of reasonable and anticipatory adjustment applied to studios, live projects, group work, hybrid learning and flexible assessment formats, with making itself accepted as evidence (D1, 1.17 to 1.24; 3.13; 3.20)

sustainability as an ethical frame for creative practice: regenerative design, circularity, responsible digital practice and the cost of GenAI, with a sustainability literacy row in Table 1 (D1, 1.25 to 1.33; 1.49; 4.4)

named employability, entrepreneurship and enterprise education: resilient, self-employed and IP-led creative careers, live projects and placements, a skills list in 1.40, and two rows of Table 1 (D1, 1.34 to 1.40; 3.16; 4.4)

GenAI as one tool in creative workflows: a spectrum from automation to refusal, students taking their own position, authentic assessment with process documentation, bias and cultural visibility, environmental cost and intellectual property (D1, 1.41 to 1.50)

subjectSpecific.text: By the end of a master's, you will typically be able to bring theory, practice, technique and context to your work with rigour and method, whether the result is creative, academic or professional.
By the end of a master's, you will typically be able to use materials widely and inventively, pushing how things are made and bringing new approaches into your practice.
By the end of a master's, you will typically be able to build and use research methods and methodologies systematically to carry advanced inquiry.
By the end of a master's, you will typically be able to analyse research, your iterations and the context of your work critically and thoroughly, so your practice moves forward.

By the end of a master's, you will typically be able to bring practice, research, ideas and knowledge to a professional finish in visual, spoken or written form, in varied, complex and unpredictable settings.
By the end of a master's, you will typically be able to place your practice in a clear, critically informed context and question its ethics, responsibilities and consequences.
By the end of a master's, you will typically be able to interpret knowledge within a clearly bounded context, alert to cultural, environmental, social and political matters.
By the end of a master's, you will typically be able to use creative strategies built around equity and inclusion, answering structural injustice through design or art.

transferable.text: By the end of a master's, you will typically be able to reflect critically on your practice in a planned, purposeful way that helps you grow and innovate.
By the end of a master's, you will typically be able to use professional ways of working with confidence in a range of complex situations.
By the end of a master's, you will typically be able to work flexibly and with agility to move projects on and take a creative approach to problems.
By the end of a master's, you will typically be able to work with others, taking the initiative, responding and leading, to reach shared goals and make a positive difference.

Accessibility and the needs of disabled students

statements.appliesTo: higher education providers offering the subject
statements.about: reasonable and anticipatory adjustments for disabled students
statements.paraphrase: Under the Equality Act 2010 providers must adjust reasonably so disabled students take a full part in academic life; in this subject that means flexible materials and structures, adjustments made in advance, and adjustments in group and collaborative work.

forPractitioner.text: Plan adjustments before they are asked for: providers must make reasonable adjustments under the Equality Act 2010, and here that means briefs shared early, other formats for lectures and content, one-to-one help or specialist kit, and adjustments for group work.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a legal duty on the provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Distinctive features of Art and Design

statements.appliesTo: students on an honours or integrated master's course
statements.about: progression across levels towards the threshold skills
statements.paraphrase: An Art and Design student will move from level to level under each institution's rules, each level adding knowledge, expertise and experience towards meeting the threshold (and any higher) subject and generic skills, usually by passing and gaining credit for all learning and assessment, practical work included.

forPractitioner.text: Map each level so that it builds towards the threshold skills in Table 1: students will progress level by level under your regulations, normally by passing and earning credit for every part of the course, practical components included.

forBeneficiary.text: You will move up one level at a time, each year adding knowledge, expertise and experience that build towards the subject and general skills expected at the end; usually that means passing and earning credit for all your learning and assessment, practical work included.

headingPath: Distinctive features of Art and Design

statements.appliesTo: students taking the subject in a joint or combined degree
statements.about: joint and combined degrees
statements.paraphrase: Students who take Art and Design within a joint or combined degree, major and minor included, will reach the core of the subject and generic skills set out here and will add others from their other subject; they may also work where the disciplines overlap.

forPractitioner.text: In a joint or combined course, students will meet the core subject and generic skills of this statement and add skills from the partner subject; design the course so the overlap between the two can be explored.

forBeneficiary.text: If you study the subject alongside another in a joint or combined degree, you will reach the core subject and general skills and add others from your second subject, with chances to explore where the two meet.

headingPath: Distinctive features of Art and Design

statements.appliesTo: degree-awarding bodies and their partners
statements.about: student voice in monitoring and review
statements.paraphrase: Degree-awarding bodies and their partners collect and analyse information and review courses periodically to their own needs; taking account of what students say will form part of this, alongside external reference points such as this statement.

forPractitioner.text: In monitoring and periodic review, students' views will form part of the evidence, read with external reference points including this statement.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the awarding body in its review process

headingPath: Distinctive features of Art and Design

statements.appliesTo: higher education providers
statements.about: external reviewers in periodic review
statements.paraphrase: Externality is essential to UK quality assurance: providers will bring in external reviewers in periodic review, for an independent view of proposed changes and to make sure threshold standards are met and the content suits the subject.

forPractitioner.text: Bring external reviewers into periodic review: they will give an independent view of changes and check that threshold standards are reached and content fits the subject.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider in periodic review

statements.appliesTo: higher education providers awarding honours
statements.about: Annex D for evidence of classification
statements.paraphrase: Most students will perform well above the minimum; each provider decides what counts as evidence of that and should consult Annex D of the 2024 Frameworks, which describes the four honours classes.

forPractitioner.text: Most students will go well beyond threshold. When deciding what evidence shows achievement, providers should use Annex D's descriptions of the first, upper second, lower second and third classes.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider in classifying degrees

statements.appliesTo: providers who develop competence standards
statements.about: competence standards and Equality and Human Rights Commission guidance
statements.paraphrase: Threshold standards are not universal competence standards; a provider that sets competence standards under the Equality Act 2010 may draw on this statement and any PSRB requirements, and should follow the latest guidance from the Equality and Human Rights Commission.

forPractitioner.text: Do not treat Table 1's threshold as a competence standard. If you write competence standards for a programme specification, draw on this statement and PSRB requirements and follow the Equality and Human Rights Commission's current guidance.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider in writing competence standards
